messages.subject: modelling residual variance
parts:
I'm trying to recreate something I've read in an article and I don't seem to figure it out, how to do it. 

Minimal example: One LV was measured 3 times and it's assumed to be influenced by a stable and a variant component (e.g. state-trait). Therefor I'd like to create one "stable" factor and three "change"-variables (which capture for each of the three waves what the one stable factor cannot account for) and use those variables for later analysis. 

minimal <- '
  # my lv measured three times 
  time1 =~ item1_1 + item2_1 + item3_1
  time2 =~ item1_2 + item2_2 + item3_2
  time3 =~ item1_3 + item2_3 + item3_3
  
  # "a" included for illustration purposes
  stable =~ a*time1 + time2 + time3

  # change-var1:3: no idea... 
  change1 ## what stable cannot explain in item1; equal sqrt( 1-a^2 )

  
'

Any ideas, comments, suggestions how to create this change-variables...?

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: modelling residual variance
parts:
The "change" variables account for the residual variances (state variances) after accounting for the variance common to each occasion (trait variance).  Path diagrams of the common factor model conventionally save space by excluding circles that represent the latent unique factors, depicting only the double-headed arrows representing the (residual) variances of those unique factors.  But you can still sometimes see the unique factors explicitly depicted, with unique-factor loadings fixed to 1 and the double-headed arrows at the unique-factor circles representing the (residual) variances of the uniquenesses.  In these more complete path diagrams (see examples in KUant Guide #24, found here), there is no actual residual variance depicted for the observed-variable squares, because the total variance of the observed variables is the sum of the common and unique factors, each weighted by their associated squared factor loadings.

Software essentially specifies those hidden parameters automatically, but if you want to use the unique factors ("change" variables) for other purposes in a larger model, you simply need to explicitly assign the residual variances to named latent factors.  For it to work, you need to fix the unique-factor loading to 1, the residual variance for the indicator to 0, and freely estimate the unique-factor variance (which will be the "change" variance you want to use in your model).  Using your minimal example:

minimal <- '
  # my lv measured three times
  time1 =~ item1_1 + item2_1 + item3_1
  time2 =~ item1_2 + item2_2 + item3_2
  time3 =~ item1_3 + item2_3 + item3_3

# stability / trait / common variance
  stable =~ time1 + time2 + time3

  # instability / state / change variance
  change1 =~ 1*time1
  change2 =~ 1*time2
  change3 =~ 1*time3
  time1 ~~ 0*time1
  time2 ~~ 0*time2
  time3 ~~ 0*time3
  change1 ~~ NA*change1
  change2 ~~ NA*change2
  change3 ~~ NA*change3
'

By default, lavaan already fixes the factor loading to 1 and estimates the factor variance for single-indicator constructs, unless you use std.lv = TRUE, but I included those parameters explicitly because I didn't know how you preferred to set the scale for your other latent variables, and this way it will work even if you specify std.lv = TRUE.

Terry
